headline: A clean first taper week — volume down sharply, the sharpener 3 sec/km quicker than target, recovery trend flipping from "lengthening" to "stable", achilles silent, aerobic base holding on both clean decoupling readings since last week. Hold the plan.
review_md:
# Weekly review — Sunday 13 September 2026

Shep — first, a quick loop-closer before the week itself. Tuesday's reply on
the 25 Oct 10K / Guy Fawkes 5 / club record question laid out the trade-off
(one target, not two, given six days between them) and left the actual
call with you. Nothing's landed back on that since, and nothing needs to —
it doesn't touch this week or race week, so it can sit until you've decided
whether it's the 10K or the record this autumn. Just flagging it so it
doesn't quietly fall off the list.

**Week of 7–13 September. Taper week 1 of 2. 7 days to Cheltenham.**

## How the week actually went

| | This week | Last week | Week before |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volume | 51.9 km | 69.2 km | 75.2 km |
| Runs | 6 | 8 | 7 |
| Quality time | 89 min | 146 min | 148 min |
| Easy share | 64% | 58% | 58% |
| Efficiency | 1.501 | 1.473 | 1.445 |
| Avg RPE | 3.0 | 2.0 | 3.4 |
| Avg HRV | 41.1 | 38.7 | — |
| Avg RHR | 46.6 | 47.6 | — |
| Avg sleep score | 86.9 | 88.4 | — |

Plan called for 51.9 km (rest, easy 8, intervals 11, easy 6, easy 5, tempo
8, long 14) and you ran exactly that — `on_target_pct` 100, no surprises in
either direction. This is the first week where the drop in volume is the
point, not a deviation from it.

Session-by-session, from `session_detail.json`:

- **Mon 8 Sep (easy, 8 km):** 8.02 km, avg HR 137. On target, nothing to
  add.
- **Wed 9 Sep (intervals, planned 11 km @ 3:44/km reps — last full
  interval session of the block):** 3.33 km warm-up, 4×1km at **3:41,
  3:44, 3:40, 3:45** (mean 3:42/km), spread 4.6 sec/km, drift **+4.0**
  (slight fade — last rep the slowest of the four), 2.98 km cool-down,
  11.04 km total vs 11 km planned. This is the session already worked
  through in Tuesday's mid-week reply: on target on three of four reps and
  dead on the fourth, RPE 7 despite a clean readiness picture that morning
  (HRV above baseline, RHR flat, ACWR 0.8). The actual lap data now
  confirms what the reply inferred from your note — a genuine but modest
  fade, consistent with cumulative fatigue from the block rather than a
  bad day, landing on the one day that kind of cost was still being asked
  of you. Nothing new here; the answer stands.
- **Thu 10 Sep (easy, 6 km) — taper begins:** 6.01 km, avg HR 137. On
  target.
- **Fri 11 Sep (easy, 5 km):** 5.31 km, RPE 1. On target.
- **Sat 12 Sep (tempo sharpener, planned 8 km, 15 min @ HM pace
  3:54/km):** 2.01 km warm-up, then a single continuous 15-minute block at
  **3:51/km** (231.0 sec/km) — 3 sec/km quicker than target — 2.10 km
  cool-down, 8.01 km total, matching the plan exactly. RPE 6. Your note:
  "Windy…was on a 1.7k loop one way was head wind, other was tail wind" —
  a net-zero wind day, so the pace stands on its own merits. This is
  exactly what a sharpener should look like eight days out: short, sharp,
  slightly ahead of target, finishing with something left rather than
  emptied.
- **Sun 13 Sep (long, planned 14 km easy — last longer run before the
  race):** 13.51 km, avg HR 147, RPE 5. Decoupling **+1.12%**, comfortably
  inside the 5% threshold — the one flag on it is `gradient_m_per_km:
  32.3` (a genuinely hilly route today), not the pacing, and first-half vs
  second-half pace and HR were both essentially flat (4:32 @ 147.1 →
  4:33 @ 148.6). The HR here (147) reads higher than a typical taper easy
  run, but between the climbing and your own note — "really muggy, felt
  like you had to chew the air" — on a day with 92% humidity, that's fully
  explained by conditions, not fatigue or drift. Achilles 0.

## How he's coping — data and his own words

Recovery markers moved the right way for a taper week: HRV 38.7→**41.1**
(up), RHR 47.6→**46.6** (down), sleep score 88.4→86.9 (flat, within
noise). `recovery_log.json`'s trend read — "lengthening" for the last two
weeks — now reads **"stable"** (recent average 3.0 days vs prior 3.3), and
every session logged this week that's old enough to score shows
`recovered: true`. That watch item from the last two reviews has resolved
itself rather than developed into a real pattern, which is the read you'd
want heading into the second taper week.

This morning's HRV (36, 4.4 points below the 7-day baseline of 40.4) is
the only outlier in the window, with no confounder logged. Same read as
always with an unexplained single-day dip: it didn't show up in execution
(RPE 5, clean flat decoupling on a muggy, hilly run) and there's nothing
to act on unless it repeats. Worth watching into Tuesday, not worth
treating as anything today.

## Achilles

0 every day this week, no mention in any note. Load is dropping now, not
rising, so this isn't the week the brief's early-warning check matters
most — but worth a plain confirmation anyway heading into race week: any
first-steps stiffness or standing-desk ache since Wednesday's last hard
session? If genuinely nothing, that's the picture you want walking into
the start line.

## Aerobic durability

The two clean, comparable decoupling readings since the last review both
sit well inside the 5% threshold: **-0.46%** (6 Sep long run, 111 minutes
analysed) and **+1.12%** (today, hilly route). Consistent with the
standing read — the aerobic base is holding steady, not sliding, at
exactly the point in the block where you'd most want reassurance rather
than a surprise. Weekly efficiency (1.501) ticked up from last week's
1.473, but that's the taper doing what a taper does — less accumulated
fatigue, sharper legs — not a fitness signal to bank on top of the
decoupling read.

## Heat and asthma

Today carried high heat risk on paper (20.8°C, but 92% humidity is the
real story) with no breathing complaint — consistent with the whole
block. The forecast through the coming week cools sharply: high risk
today and tomorrow, then **low heat risk from Wednesday 16th through
Saturday 19th** (17–17°C, humidity dropping to 69–76%). The window doesn't
yet reach race day itself — the 7-day pull stops one day short of the
20th — but the trend is the right one to be seeing a week out, especially
given the Cotswold Way history.

That also puts a number on the asthma-preventer timing question you
raised yourself two weeks ago. Inhaled steroid preventers work
cumulatively over weeks, and today is effectively the last point at which
starting one would do anything meaningful before Saturday's gun — from
here it's a decision about ongoing management past Cheltenham, not race
prep. That's still a call for your GP or asthma nurse, not this brief, so
if you haven't had that conversation yet, today or tomorrow is the moment,
otherwise it naturally becomes a post-Cheltenham decision instead. Either
way, nothing new should start in race week itself.

## Race plan — Cheltenham Half Marathon, Sat 20 Sep

You asked for this last Sunday once Wednesday's intervals were done and
the taper was underway — both true now, so here it is.

**Pacing.** The plan already has the right shape written into race day:
first 5 km no faster than 3:56/km, target 1:21–1:23, the model
independently landing on 1:22:23–1:22:25 (range 1:20:11–1:24:38) off your
current 5K/10K. That's a race won after 15 km, not before 5 — start
conservative relative to feel, and let the effort curve up as the
prediction's own confidence band would suggest is safe to do. One honest
gap: I don't have a course-profile file for Cheltenham, so I can't tell
you where the hills are or whether it's a fast, flat course or a rolling
one. If you know the route, that's worth five minutes before Saturday —
effort should govern any rise or fall, not the pace band.

**Conditions.** As above — cooling and drying through the week, favourable
trend, exact race-day numbers not available until the forecast window
reaches the 20th (likely by Tuesday or Wednesday's pull).

**Shoes.** Puma Fast-R Nitro 3 is the confirmed racing shoe. The plan
flagged 5 Sep's tempo as a good day for a dress rehearsal in them, but
there's no shoe mentioned in that day's note, so I can't confirm it
happened. Worth a straight answer: have you raced or run quality in the
Fast-R 3s recently? If not, Tuesday's 6×400m at HM rhythm (16 Sep) is the
last realistic chance to put them on for something other than an easy
run before Saturday.

**Protocol.** Symbicort 20 min before the gun, salbutamol 15 min before —
already in the plan for race day, unchanged.

## Race countdown

7 days to Cheltenham (1.0 weeks). Prediction unchanged in substance:
**1:22:25** (range 1:20:11–1:24:38) against your 1:21–1:23 target. Zero
remaining key sessions — Wednesday's intervals were the last of those.
Everything left is taper: rest, easy 6 + strides (Tue 15), easy 8 with
6×400m at rhythm (Wed 16), easy 5 (Thu 17), rest (Fri 18), easy 4 +
strides (Sat 19), race (Sun 20).

## Recommendation: **hold**

Nothing to change. This week did exactly what a first taper week should:
volume down sharply (51.9 km vs 69.2 km), quality protected and sharp
(the sharpener came in 3 sec/km quicker than target), recovery trending
the right way rather than lingering as a worry, achilles silent, aerobic
base holding on the two clean decoupling readings since last week. The
plan for the second taper week is already written and doesn't need
touching.

Two things worth a plain answer before Saturday, neither a plan change:
any achilles stiffness since Wednesday, and whether you've had quality
minutes in the Fast-R Nitro 3s recently.

athlete_response.thoughts: Race start is 9am. Plan for breakfast. Usually have bowl of rice crispies, bagel with honey, coffee and then sipping sis isotonic drink on way to race

coach_reply:
Shep — that plan is right, and it's right for the reason that matters most this close in: it's what you already do, not something new for the start line. Rice krispies, bagel with honey and coffee is literally the brief's own pre-long-run breakfast, and a familiar coffee before a race you've raced this distance before isn't a novel stimulus — so there's nothing here to caution against.

On timing: with a 9am gun, eat the solid breakfast around 2.5–3h out — roughly 6:00–6:30am — so it's properly digested rather than sitting heavy at the start line. Sipping the SiS isotonic on the way in closer to the gun tops you up without adding volume this late, which is exactly the right shape.

Worth knowing, not changing: at today's 1:22:25 prediction this race sits in the 75–100 minute bracket, where the brief's carbohydrate table treats a gel or carb drink during the run itself as "for practice rather than need" — a race this length runs fine off a solid breakfast and pre-race carb alone. So the isotonic sipping is generous rather than essential, and that's not a problem, just context for why you won't feel like you're under-fuelled even though it's a light amount for the distance. Nothing to add or strip out.

No change to the plan. Achilles read 0 again today, the 4km + strides went exactly to plan, and the breakfast routine you've described is proven, not experimental — you're set for tomorrow.

conversation.athlete_thoughts:
No issues with achillies at any point... Something to bear in mind after Cheltenham.
Yes I've run in the fast rs when the plan said too.  I will also get a route elevation update for you
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — good, that closes out both open questions cleanly. Achilles at 0 all week lines up with `computed_data.json`, and the Fast-R 3 confirmation means the dress rehearsal happened even though it didn't make it into the note — both boxes ticked, nothing to act on.

"Something to bear in mind after Cheltenham" is the right instinct, and it's worth saying why rather than just nodding at it. There's no plan written past race day yet, and the next real decision on the calendar is how fast volume climbs toward Manchester — sub-3 off your current ~60–65 km norm is possible but thin, and that conversation belongs in the autumn, which is where we are. Four years of achilles history says the constraint on that ramp isn't fitness, it's how quickly load rises and how well it's run — exactly the two things a clean taper into a well-run half won't tell you anything about on their own. So it's not a flag on anything happening now; it's the right thing to be tracking as the first input into how the post-Cheltenham build gets shaped, and it'll be there when that conversation starts.

Route elevation — yes please, and it'll go straight into the race plan once it lands. Right now the pacing note says effort should govern any hills since I can't see the profile; with the elevation data I can actually tell you where to expect that rather than leaving it to feel on the day.

No change to the plan. Still hold — second taper week runs as written.

Shep — approved and logged, though there's nothing here for the gate to actually apply: the review's recommendation was hold, so there's no proposal sitting behind this approval. It just confirms you're happy with the second taper week running as written, which it will.

That's the right call on the evidence, not just the mood. Recovery trend flipped from lengthening to stable this week, achilles read 0 every day with no stiffness on direct question, the sharpener came in 3 sec/km quicker than target, and both clean decoupling readings since last review sat well inside the 5% threshold. Nothing in that picture asks for a change, and race week plans — rest, easy 6 + strides, easy 8 with 6×400m at rhythm, easy 5, rest, easy 4 + strides, race — stay exactly as written.

One thing's already moved since this morning's review: the elevation update you mentioned has made it into `training_plan.json` — Saturday's entry now carries gradient-adjusted splits (downhill start capped at 3:56, effort-not-pace through the two climbs at 6km and 12km, hold through the climb at 20km, empty it on the downhill last km). That closes the one open gap the review flagged, so the race-day plan is complete, not just a pace band.

Nothing left to decide before Saturday. Go run it.

conversation.athlete_thoughts: today is a rest day - but can i just sauna?
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — yes, go ahead. Today's rest, no session behind it, so there's nothing to compound: none of the load-management logic in the plan is about deliberately layering extra stress onto a day that's already designed to have none.

On the asthma point specifically: the Cotswold Way episode was heat *combined with* hard exercise — it's the ventilation demand of running hard in the heat that drives exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Sitting in a sauna doesn't carry that ventilation load, so it isn't really a repeat of that trigger, and today's recovery numbers back up that there's no reason to treat it as anything but a low-stress day either way — HRV 42 (right on the 41.1 baseline), RHR 47, sleep score 94.

One thing to be straight about, so you don't overrate it: a single sauna session 6 days out won't do anything for heat acclimation — that needs repeated post-exercise exposures over 1–2 weeks, which isn't the window you've got left before Saturday. So treat it as what it is today — recovery, not race prep — keep it moderate rather than pushing duration or heat, and rehydrate properly afterwards; the sweat loss is real even without running. I'd also leave it at today rather than making it a daily fixture through race week — no benefit to repeating it this close in, and it's one more variable on your fluid and electrolyte status heading into Saturday that you don't need.

No change to the plan — this isn't a training question, it's a recovery-day one, and the answer's yes with the caveats above.

conversation.athlete_thoughts: yeah just wasnt sure if rest meant nothing at all or would a sauna be fine.  it is so i may do so.  of note is that i will generally have a sauna after a run and then time in a hydro pool too.  not all the time but if ive run from david lloyd its highly likely
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — that context actually settles it rather than raising anything new. Sauna-then-hydro-pool after a David Lloyd run being your normal pattern, not something you're introducing this week, is the important bit: the caution about heat exposure in race week is about *novel* stimulus — a new shoe, a new recovery habit, anything the body hasn't already absorbed — and this isn't that. Doing what you always do after a David Lloyd run, this week included, is the "nothing new" option. Stopping it because it's race week would be the actual change.

Two caveats, both about degree, not principle. First — is the hydro pool warm or cold? Most gym hydro pools (David Lloyd's included, generally) are warm hydrotherapy, in which case this is straightforward recovery with no downside for endurance training. If it's a cold plunge, that's a different question — cold water immersion has decent evidence for blunting adaptation when used right after a hard session, though that evidence is stronger for strength work than for running, and it's a smaller concern this close to a race than it would be mid-block anyway. Second — run plus sauna plus pool is three sources of fluid loss stacked together, so rehydrate and replace electrolytes for that total, not just the run, particularly after Wednesday's rhythm session and however you time it in the two days before Saturday.

No change to the plan — this doesn't touch `training_plan.json`, and the second taper week runs exactly as written.

conversation.athlete_thoughts: as i mention its not every run but i do use sauna and hydro quite a bit.probably more in the winter than sumer.  i stopped the cold plunge along time ago probably after chatting with you. and yes i do hydrate if doing run and sauna
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — that settles both caveats from the last reply cleanly. Not a cold plunge — you dropped that a while back, which tracks with what we discussed then — so the hydro pool is warm hydrotherapy, not the cold-immersion scenario that would've been worth a second thought this close to a race. And you're hydrating for the combination, not just the run. Both boxes ticked, nothing to act on.

The winter-more-than-summer pattern is worth noting for what it implies, not for anything to change: it means the extra fluid loss this combination adds is highest exactly when heat risk is already lowest, and lowest when heat risk is highest — so the two broadly offset rather than stack. Today's numbers back up that the rest-day sauna isn't costing you anything either way: HRV 42 (right on the 41.1 baseline), RHR 47, sleep score 94, all normal for a taper rest day.

No change to the plan — today stays rest, second taper week runs exactly as written.

conversation.athlete_thoughts: I'm sure I read somewhere, don't have a hot bath the day before a race. You want your tendons to be fired up, whereas a hot bath will do the opposite. If so should I avoid the sauna and hydropool Saturday
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — the mechanism you're describing is real, but the timing doesn't work the way the folk version says it does. Heat does increase collagen extensibility — it's literally why a warm-up works and why heated stretching is more effective than cold stretching. But that effect is local and short-lived: tendon and muscle temperature return to baseline within roughly an hour or two of the heat source being removed, not overnight. Saturday's sauna and hydropool, however long you're in for, will have zero measurable effect on achilles or any other tendon stiffness by Sunday morning — that's 12–15+ hours later, several tissue-cooling half-lives beyond where any compliance change persists. If sauna-the-day-before genuinely blunted race-day tendon spring, distance runners who train at facilities with saunas attached would have found that out a long time ago.

So I'm not going to tell you to skip it on that basis — there's no evidence behind the specific claim, and achilles has read 0 every day this taper with nothing in any note, so there's no vulnerability here that heat exposure would be interacting with anyway.

The part of this worth actually managing isn't tendon mechanics, it's fluid balance — the same point from Sunday's exchange about hydrating for the run-plus-sauna-plus-pool combination, just closer to the start line now. Saturday is the one day this week you most want to toe the line fully topped up rather than still catching up on fluid and electrolytes lost the evening before, and Saturday's session is easy 4km + strides, not a rest day, so any sauna/hydro after it stacks on top of that. That's not a reason to cut it — it's your normal post-run pattern, not something novel, and novel is what the taper actually needs to avoid — just keep it to your usual length rather than lingering, and rehydrate properly afterwards so you're not making up the deficit on race morning instead.

No change to the plan. This is a logistics call, not a training one — second taper week runs exactly as written, race day plan unchanged.

conversation.athlete_thoughts: what speed are the 400s? HMP pace?
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — yes, HM rhythm. Same number as Saturday's race and the sharpener: **3:54/km** (your 3:52–3:56/km band), not Wednesday's 3:44/km 10K-pace reps. Over 400m that's ~93–94 sec, so **1:33–1:34 per rep**.

That's deliberately not a repeat of last Wednesday's quality — it's a taper leg-speed opener, four days out: short reps at exactly the pace you'll hold on Saturday, with plenty of jog recovery, to groove the rhythm rather than add another hard session this late. The plan note says "effort light" for a reason — if hitting 1:33 takes work rather than floating there, ease off half a second a rep. This is the last chance to rehearse race pace before the start line, not a session to find out if you're fit.

No change to the plan — Wednesday runs exactly as written.

conversation.athlete_thoughts: Really easy session. The hard part going slow over the 400s. Interesting that the Garmin watch lowered my HR on my lactate threshold to 165 but kept the pace the same
conversation.coach_reply:
Shep — both halves of that are worth taking separately, because one confirms the plan and the other isn't telling you what it looks like it's telling you.

"Really easy, the hard part was going slow" is exactly the session working as designed, not a sign the targets are stale. This morning's reply on the 400m pace said it plainly: this is a leg-speed opener at HM rhythm four days out, with plenty of jog recovery, meant to groove the rhythm rather than test fitness — "if hitting 1:33 takes work rather than floating there, ease off." Floating there and finding the discipline the hard part is the intended outcome, not underdone work. And for the record, `pace_target.json` isn't live on this one regardless: it flagged on 12 Sep, went into its three-session cooldown, and doesn't track 400m rhythm reps as a scored session type anyway — only the Wednesday interval and Saturday tempo sessions feed it. So there's no stale-target read to make here even in principle.

On the watch dropping its lactate-threshold HR estimate to 165 while holding the pace: that's Garmin's own auto-detected algorithm, not a lab test, and it isn't a number this repo pulls or tracks anywhere — `garmin_data.json` carries RHR, HRV, VO2max, training load and ACWR, nothing calling itself LTHR. Same category as running power in the brief: a vendor model, useful as corroboration, never as a primary signal to act on. And what it's corroborating here is exactly what the rest of today's numbers already say — ACWR down to 0.7 ("LOW"), VO2max steady at 60, training status "PRODUCTIVE_3": you're fresh, so the same pace now costs a lower estimated HR than it did mid-block. That's the taper doing its job, not new fitness to bank or a reason to tighten Saturday's pace band — your race splits derive from the 5K/10K results, not from a watch's rolling threshold guess, and that stays true right through the start line.

No change to the plan. Thursday's easy 5 and the rest of race week run exactly as written.
